passage:
Class UKG settling-in note. Yogesh, class teacher.
Dhruv (5), week three. He now waves at the gate and says, "Bye Mumma, come at twelve," and walks in alone. Today he spent most of free play building a tall block tower by himself, and only called me over when it fell. At 11:55 he stood at the window watching the gate. When his mother came, he ran to hug her knees for a few seconds, then ran back to show her his tower. Next: I'll tell his mother how well the quick goodbye is working, and keep the same pickup routine.

qa.q: What does Dhruv say at the gate now?
qa.a: "Bye Mumma, come at twelve."

qa.q: Why did Dhruv stand at the window at 11:55?
qa.a: He was expecting his mother and wanted to see her come, trusting she would be back at twelve.

qa.q: Why is keeping the same pickup routine a good plan?
qa.a: A reliable return is what lets Dhruv feel safe enough to play on his own.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's mother feel when he hugs her knees and then runs back to his tower?
qa.a: She may feel happy and reassured that he has settled and wants to share his school world with her.

grounding: A child settling into school says goodbye, plays alone and checks in briefly at pickup, trusting his mother will return.

passage: At the village school gate, Lakshmi let go of her mother Sangeeta's finger and marched in, tin box swinging. She didn't look back until she reached the neem tree. Then she turned, waved once and ran off to the swing. All morning she played hopscotch with two new friends. When the bell rang, she spotted Sangeeta by the gate, raced over and pressed her face into her sari for a second. Then she tugged her by the hand. "Come, see my chalk house!"

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi turn and wave?
qa.a: At the neem tree.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi pressing her face into Sangeeta's sari for a second suggest?
qa.a: She was glad and relieved to see her mother, a quick check-in before going back to sharing her day.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta keep doing to help Lakshmi feel brave at school?
qa.a: Being at the gate reliably when the bell rings, so Lakshmi keeps trusting she will come.

qa.q: What is it like for Sangeeta when Lakshmi lets go of her finger without looking back?
qa.a: It may feel proud and a little tender, watching her daughter walk off on her own.

grounding: A young girl leaves her mother at the school gate, plays freely and runs back for a quick check-in at the bell.

passage: Every morning at the kindergarten in Oslo, Lars hung his jacket on the hook with the fox sticker and asked, "Pappa, you come after snack two?" Daniel nodded. "After snack two." Lars hugged him fast and went straight to the sandpit. He dug a river with a new boy, argued about a bucket and made up. When Daniel came through the gate that afternoon, Lars dropped his spade, ran over, hugged his legs hard, then dragged him to the sandpit. "Look, a river! Now go wait there."

qa.q: What sticker is on Lars's hook?
qa.a: A fox sticker.

qa.q: Why does Lars ask "Pappa, you come after snack two?" every morning?
qa.a: Hearing when his father will return helps him feel safe enough to say goodbye and play.

qa.q: What is helpful about Daniel repeating "After snack two"?
qa.a: It gives Lars a clear, reliable promise, so he can trust his father will come back and venture out.

qa.q: How might Daniel feel being told "Now go wait there"?
qa.a: Probably amused and pleased, since it shows Lars feels secure enough to send him off again 😊

grounding: A kindergartner says goodbye, plays independently and runs back for a quick hug at pickup, knowing his father will return.

passage:
At the school gate on his tenth morning, Lalit, five, held out his palm. Papa Saurabh pressed a pretend kiss into it, and Lalit closed his fist and put it in his pocket, their daily ritual. "Pickup at one?" "At one, by the banyan tree." Lalit waved once and ran in without looking back.
In the sandpit he built a long road with a spoon, alone, humming. At one he spotted Papa under the banyan, dashed over, touched his knee and said, "Wait, my road isn't finished." Then he ran back to finish it.

qa.q: Where did Papa say he would be at pickup?
qa.a: By the banyan tree.

qa.q: Why do you think Lalit could run in without looking back?
qa.a: He trusted that Papa would be there at one, and the pocket kiss helped him feel safe enough to go.

qa.q: What makes the pocket-kiss ritual helpful for a child settling in?
qa.a: It gives Lalit a small, reliable goodbye and a promise of return, which makes separating easier.

qa.q: How might Papa Saurabh feel when Lalit touches his knee and runs back to his road?
qa.a: He may feel happy and a little amused that Lalit feels secure enough to check in and go straight back to play.

grounding: A five-year-old settling into school waves goodbye, plays alone and makes a quick check-in at pickup, trusting his father will return.

passage:
I'm Manoj, and I wait at the playschool gate every noon for my granddaughter, so I've watched little Raghav, four, all term. In June he cried and clung to his mother's dupatta. By August he said, "Bye Mumma, see you at twelve," and walked in alone.
I can't know what he feels, but I see him in the play corner driving a toy bus along the wall, talking to it. When the bell goes, he runs to the gate, touches his mother's hand, shows her a paper boat, and then runs back for his bus.

qa.q: What did Raghav drive along the wall in the play corner?
qa.a: A toy bus.

qa.q: What might Raghav's quick touch of his mother's hand suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels safe to explore but still likes to check that his mother, his safe base, is there.

qa.q: How could Raghav's mother support his growing independence?
qa.a: By keeping her twelve o'clock promise every day, so he trusts she will return and keeps venturing out.

qa.q: What might Raghav's mother feel seeing him walk in alone after June's tears?
qa.a: She may feel proud and a little wistful that he needs her less at the gate.

grounding: A grandfather at the gate watches a four-year-old go from clinging to waving goodbye, playing alone and checking in at pickup.

passage: Every morning at the school gate in Lisbon, Paulo, five, hugs his dad Daniel's legs, then lets go. "Bye, Papá!" He runs to the sandpit without looking back and builds tunnels with a new friend all morning. At three o'clock, the gate opens. Paulo spots Daniel, races over, bumps into his knees, shows him a sandy hand, then runs straight back to finish his tunnel.

qa.q: What does Paulo build in the sandpit?
qa.a: He builds tunnels with a new friend.

qa.q: Why can Paulo run off without looking back?
qa.a: Paulo feels safe and confident because he trusts Daniel will be there at three o'clock.

qa.q: What could Daniel keep doing to support Paulo's confidence?
qa.a: Daniel can keep coming at the same time and greeting Paulo's quick check-ins warmly, so Paulo keeps feeling secure enough to explore.

qa.q: How might Daniel feel when Paulo runs back to the tunnel after a quick hug?
qa.a: Daniel may feel a little wistful but mostly proud and reassured that Paulo is settling in well.

grounding: A child settling into school waves goodbye, plays on his own and runs back for a quick check-in at pickup because his father reliably returns.

passage: At Tiny Tots kindergarten, Lavanya's Appa, Zubin, crouches at the classroom door. "I'll be back after lunch, like always." Lavanya, four, nods, waves, and trots to the painting table. She paints a blue sun, then plays shop with two girls. When the bell rings, she spots Zubin at the door and races over. She hugs his neck, tells him about the blue sun, then tugs away. "Wait, Appa! I have to finish selling!" He laughs and waits.

qa.q: What colour sun does Lavanya paint?
qa.a: Lavanya paints a blue sun.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's quick hug and tug away suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels secure and happy, reassured Appa is back so she can go on playing.

qa.q: Why does Zubin's "I'll be back after lunch, like always" help?
qa.a: The steady promise, kept every day, helps Lavanya trust that he returns, which frees her to play on her own.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Lavanya's quick check-in at pickup?
qa.a: The teacher might see it as a healthy sign that Lavanya has settled and uses her father as a safe base.

grounding: A child in kindergarten waves goodbye, plays independently and runs back for a quick check-in at pickup, trusting her father to return.

passage:
First day: Bidisha, five, cries at the school gate and grips Baba's shirt. Raghav kneels. "I'll be right here at one." She goes in, sniffling.
Third day: She waves at the gate, then peeps back twice from the corridor. At one, Raghav is there. She runs to him and holds tight.
Second week: Bidisha waves and skips straight in. At pickup she runs over, taps his hand, says "Wait!" and dashes back to finish a skipping game.

qa.q: What time does Raghav promise to be there?
qa.a: He promises to be right there at one.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling on the first day at the gate?
qa.a: Bidisha felt scared and anxious, crying and gripping Baba's shirt.

qa.q: What helped Bidisha feel brave enough to skip straight in by the second week?
qa.a: Raghav kept his promise every day, so she learnt she could trust him to return and felt safe exploring.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel when Bidisha taps his hand and runs back to her game?
qa.a: Raghav may feel proud and a little amused, seeing how confident she has become.

grounding: Over two weeks, a child settling into school learns to wave goodbye, play on her own and use quick check-ins because her father reliably returns.

passage:
It was the first day after the summer holidays, and the school gate in Hyderabad was crowded and hot. Vishal, five, held his mother Dilnaz's hand tight.
"I'll be right here at one o'clock," she said. "Same gate."
Vishal nodded, waved, and ran in. All morning he played with the blocks and sang in circle time.
At one o'clock, he burst out, ran straight to Dilnaz, hugged her legs for three seconds, and then pulled her to see the painting he'd made. "Come see!"
Knowing she'd be at the gate had made the whole morning easy.

qa.q: What time did Dilnaz promise to be at the gate?
qa.a: At one o'clock.

qa.q: Why could Vishal wave and run in so easily?
qa.a: He felt safe and trusting, knowing his mother would be back at the same gate.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do that helped Vishal venture out?
qa.a: She gave a clear promise about when and where she'd be, and kept it.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel when Vishal hugs her and drags her to see his painting?
qa.a: She probably feels happy and relieved that he enjoyed school and still ran to her.

grounding: A child settling into school waves goodbye, plays alone and runs back for a quick hug, trusting his mother will return.

passage:
It was the first cold week of winter at the Chandigarh kindergarten, and Minakshi, four, wore her new red sweater. At the door, her father Baljeet knelt.
"I'll be here at pickup. By the swing."
Minakshi waved and ran in. She painted, played house and ate her lunch without once looking back.
At pickup, she dashed to the swing where Baljeet stood. She touched his hand, grinned, then ran back to finish a game of tag.
Baljeet laughed. "Just checking I'm here?"
Minakshi nodded and ran off again.

qa.q: Where did Baljeet say he'd be at pickup?
qa.a: By the swing.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi run to touch Baljeet's hand and then run off again?
qa.a: She felt safe and reassured seeing he was there, so she could go back to playing.

qa.q: How did Baljeet's promise help Minakshi?
qa.a: Knowing where he'd be made it easy for her to play independently all day.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel when Minakshi runs back to her game?
qa.a: He probably feels amused and proud that she feels secure enough to go off again.

grounding: A child plays independently at kindergarten and runs for a quick check-in at pickup, trusting her father will be there.

passage:
"Ammi, will you come back?" Zeenat, five, asked at the school gate on the first day after the Eid holidays.
"Of course. At two o'clock. With your brother Suraj."
"Promise?"
"Promise."
Zeenat waved and ran in. She played with clay, sang songs, and forgot to look back.
At two, she spotted Ammi and Suraj at the gate. She ran, hugged them both, then said, "Wait, I want to show my clay cat!" and ran back inside to get it.
Ammi laughed. "She's fine."
"She just wanted to see us," said Suraj.

qa.q: What time did Ammi promise to come back?
qa.a: At two o'clock.

qa.q: Why could Zeenat forget to look back while playing?
qa.a: She felt safe and trusting because Ammi had promised to come back.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that helped Zeenat go in happily?
qa.a: She answered her question clearly with a time and a promise.

qa.q: How does Suraj understand Zeenat's quick hug?
qa.a: Suraj sees that she just wanted to check they were there before running off again.

grounding: A child waves goodbye at school, plays independently and runs back for a quick check-in, trusting her mother will return.

passage:
KG note, first week back after the Diwali holidays.
On Monday Gopika clung to her mother, Ankita, at the gate for ten minutes. Ankita promised, 'I'll be here at twelve, by the neem tree,' and left. By Wednesday Gopika waved goodbye herself and ran to the sand tray, humming. Twice she looked towards the gate, then went back to digging. At pickup today she raced to the neem tree, hugged Ankita's knees for a few seconds, then ran back to show me her sandcastle. I suggested Ankita keep the goodbye short and the same each day.

qa.q: Where did Ankita promise to wait at twelve?
qa.a: By the neem tree.

qa.q: What does Gopika looking towards the gate and then going back to digging suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Gopika felt secure enough to play, trusting that her mother would come back.

qa.q: Why is keeping the goodbye short and the same each day helpful?
qa.a: A predictable goodbye reminds Gopika her mother always returns, which makes it easier to go off and play.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Gopika runs back to show the sandcastle?
qa.a: Ankita likely feels relieved and proud, seeing her daughter confident enough to leave her again after a quick hug.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young girl venturing into play because she trusts her mother will return, with a quick check-in at pickup.

passage: At the Pongal fair in the village, bullocks with painted horns stood by the temple tank, and Charu wanted to see all of them. Her Appa, Chinmay, sat on the steps with the sugarcane. 'Go with your cousins. I'll be right here.' Charu ran off, then stopped at the first bullock, turned round, found Appa's white shirt on the steps, and waved. He waved back. She went further, to the balloon man, then ran all the way back just to touch his knee. 'You're here.' 'I'm here.' Off she went again, braver each time.

qa.q: Where did Chinmay sit?
qa.a: On the steps with the sugarcane.

qa.q: Why did Charu run back just to touch Appa's knee?
qa.a: Charu wanted a quick moment of safety; touching him made her feel secure enough to go further.

qa.q: What did Chinmay's 'I'll be right here' do for Charu?
qa.a: It gave her a fixed, safe spot to return to, which made exploring the fair possible.

qa.q: What is it like for Chinmay watching Charu go further each time?
qa.a: Chinmay probably feels proud and content, seeing his daughter grow braver while knowing she can always come back.

grounding: At a village festival a young girl explores further each time after quick check-ins with her father as a safe base.

passage: The rainy season had started in Lagos, and Gabriel's new school smelled of wet shoes. On Monday he held his father Emeka's hand so tightly it left marks. 'I'll come back at two, when the big bell rings,' Emeka said, kneeling to fix his collar. Gabriel let go slowly. By Thursday he walked in alone, turned at the classroom door and waved like a grown-up. At two o'clock he spotted Emeka under the umbrella, ran over, pressed his face into his father's raincoat for three seconds, then pulled him inside to see the paper boat he had made.

qa.q: When did Emeka promise to come back?
qa.a: At two, when the big bell rings.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling on Monday?
qa.a: Gabriel felt anxious about being left, holding his father's hand so tightly it left marks.

qa.q: What helped Gabriel become confident by Thursday?
qa.a: Emeka's clear, kept promise to return at two taught Gabriel he could go in and his father would be there.

qa.q: How might Emeka feel when Gabriel pulls him inside to see the boat?
qa.a: Emeka probably feels relieved and proud that his son now goes in alone and wants to share his day.

grounding: In the rainy season abroad a young boy settles into school, trusting his father's return, and checks in at pickup.

At pickup she spots Mamma's umbrella, races across the wet yard, crashes into her knees for one quick squeeze, then runs off again. "Wait! I have to show you Imran's tower falling down!"
